It is supposed to take the man who has kept the commandments from his youth, the best man in the room, and show him he cannot purchase his way in with obedience any more than with money. The objection that the saying is too harsh, that no rich person could be saved on these terms, is not a problem to be solved. It is the door. Because the moment you stop trying to fit the camel through the needle by your own management, by unloading the right amount of baggage and kneeling the right amount, the moment you confess the thing simply cannot be done, you are finally standing where the gospel can reach you. With man it is impossible. The impossibility is not the bad news that precedes the gospel. The impossibility is the gospel's first word of truth.

This is the cross, and it stands here as law before grace, exactly. The law is the needle. It measures you and finds you too large, too laden, too sure of your own keeping of the commandments, and it does not lie. I am the camel. I have possessions I have justified, securities I have called prudence, a comfort I would be slow to sell even to follow the One I claim to follow. The law names me before it names the man who walked away sorrowful. And then grace. The One who said it is impossible is the One who went up to Jerusalem to make the impossible happen, who became poor that we by His poverty might become rich, who was Himself the only one who could pass through the needle and chose instead to be threaded onto a Roman cross so that camels like me could follow Him through. The man walked away because he thought the price was his wealth. The price was higher than that. The price was everything, and it was paid by someone else.

So what do we do with the rich young ruler, we who are, by every global measure, richer than he ever dreamed. We stop building the gate. We let the sentence stand at its full impossible height. We let it take the breath out of us the way it took the breath out of the disciples. And then, having despaired of fitting through on our own terms, we look up at the only One for whom all things are possible, and we hear the same command the rich man heard, the command he could not obey and we cannot either, except that now it comes from a Savior who has already gone ahead of us through the needle He alone could pass.

The man went away sorrowful. The text does not tell us he never came back. I have hoped, in more than one quiet moment, that he did. That somewhere after the cross he heard that the thing he could not do had been done for him, and that he came back, lighter now, not because he had finally unloaded enough, but because he had finally stopped trying to fit and let himself be carried.

### Works Cited

John Chrysostom. On Wealth and Poverty. Translated by Catharine P. Roth. Crestwood: St. Vladimir's Seminary Press, 1984.

Keller, Timothy. Counterfeit Gods: The Empty Promises of Money, Sex, and Power, and the Only Hope That Matters. New York: Dutton, 2009.

The Holy Bible, English Standard Version. Wheaton: Crossway, 2001.

chapters.title: What Is Biblical Justice? Mishpat and Tsedaqah
chapters.summary: Biblical justice is two Hebrew words held together, and the church keeps tearing them apart.
chapters.body:
A widow comes to the gate. The gate is where the elders sit, where the cases are heard, where the field of one man is weighed against the hunger of another. She has no husband to speak for her, no son old enough, no money for the kind of voice that wins. She stands at the edge of the assembly and waits to see whether the word that comes out of that gate will be true. Everything the Bible means by justice is decided in the next ten minutes. Not in the abstract. At the gate. For her.

We have lost the gate. We argue about justice as though it were a theory, a flag, a team. The word has been pulled so far in two directions that for many in the church it now means only one of two things, either a check written to the poor or a vote cast for a party. The Bible's word for justice is older and stranger than both, and it will not fit in either pocket. To recover it we have to learn two Hebrew words and the way they are bound together, because the prophets almost never speak one without the other.

The spine of this whole question is a single verse, and I want to carry it through every turn. 'He has told you, O man, what is good, and what does the Lord require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God' (Micah 6:8 ESV). The word translated justice is mishpat. The word translated kindness, hesed, is the covenant love that keeps faith. And standing behind this verse, woven through Micah's contemporaries, is its partner, tsedaqah. Mishpat and tsedaqah. Justice and righteousness. The prophets pair them so often that to hear one is to expect the other, the way you expect a second footfall after the first. Understand the pair, and you understand what the Bible asks of us at the gate.

Start with mishpat. The simplest definition is the giving of people their due, the rectifying of wrongs, the rendering of a verdict that matches reality. Mishpat is what the elders at the gate are supposed to produce, a judgment that is true regardless of who is standing before them. But the Hebrew is wider than a courtroom. Mishpat includes punishment for the one who wronged the widow, yes, but it also includes care for the widow herself, provision, restitution, the active setting right of what was bent. It is not merely the absence of crime. It is the presence of right outcomes. When Amos thunders 'let justice roll down like waters' (Amos 5:24 ESV), the word is mishpat, and the image is not a trickle of fair verdicts. It is a flood that reaches every dry field, that carries the widow's case all the way downstream to a result she can live on.

Now tsedaqah. We translate it righteousness, and immediately we have shrunk it, because in English righteousness sounds like private virtue, a clean personal record, the moral hygiene of an individual soul. In Hebrew tsedaqah is overwhelmingly relational and social. It means living in right relationship with everyone around you, rendering to each person what the covenant says they are owed, not as a transaction but as a way of being a faithful member of a people. Tim Keller put it well, that tsedaqah is day to day right living and mishpat is rectifying justice, and the Bible welds them so that you cannot have one without the other (Keller 2010). A man could be technically blameless, breaking no law, paying no bribe, and still lack tsedaqah, because tsedaqah asks not merely whether you have done wrong but whether you have done right, whether you have used what you have to repair what is broken near you. Tsedaqah is generous, structural, and active. It is the disposition that produces mishpat as its fruit.

This is the crucial thing the two words do together. Mishpat without tsedaqah becomes mere procedure, a fair trial that no one ever helps the widow reach. Tsedaqah without mishpat becomes private charity, a generous heart that never touches the law that keeps making widows. The Hebrew binds them precisely so that neither can be amputated from the other. And amputation is exactly the church's habit. We keep choosing one word and calling it the whole.

Consider where the pairing shows up. It is not occasional. When God describes the man he chose to found a nation, the reason given is this, that Abraham would command his children and his household after him to keep the way of the Lord by doing righteousness and justice, tsedaqah and mishpat (Genesis 18:19 ESV). The two words are named as the content of the covenant before there is a covenant nation to keep it. When the Psalms describe the throne of God itself, they say righteousness and justice are the foundation of his throne (Psalm 89:14 ESV). The two words are the floor God's own rule stands on. When Isaiah grieves over the failure of Israel, he says God looked for mishpat and behold, bloodshed, for tsedaqah and behold, a cry (Isaiah 5:7 ESV). The two words are what God came looking for and did not find. This is not a marginal theme a few activists have inflated. It is the recurring description of what God is like, what God requires, and what God grieves when it is absent. To miss the pair is to misread the center of the Hebrew Scriptures.

Let me steel-man the first amputation, the one that says justice is fundamentally personal charity. This view is held by serious, faithful people, and it is not selfishness in disguise. Its argument runs deep. Charity, it says, is personal because love is personal. The Good Samaritan did not file a grievance against the Jericho road. He bent down, he bound the wounds, he paid the innkeeper out of his own pocket, he made the suffering of one man his own. The Bible's heroes of mercy are people who give, who sacrifice, who touch. And there is a guarding wisdom here. The moment you make justice a matter of policy alone, you let me off the hook of personal cost. I can vote and stay clean. I never have to bleed the man on the road, never have to know his name, never have to be inconvenienced past the ballot. The charity view is protecting the personal, sacrificial, face to face love that no government program can manufacture. It is protecting hesed, the covenant love standing right there in Micah's verse beside justice. That is real, and a justice that despises it has lost the gospel.

But here is where the strong version of the charity view fails on its own terms. The Good Samaritan is a parable about the man already beaten by the road. It is not a parable about the road. And Scripture also gives us the road. When Isaiah indicts the writers who keep writing oppression, when Amos names those who trample the head of the poor into the dust of the earth and sell the needy for a pair of sandals (Amos 2:6 to 7 ESV), the prophet is not describing a failure of charity. He is describing a market, a court, a structure, working as built. You cannot bind the wounds of a man the system beats faster than you can bandage. Tsedaqah, rightly understood, was never only personal. The covenant itself was structural. Leviticus commands the corners of every field left unharvested for the poor and the stranger, not as charity the farmer chooses but as law the harvest obeys. The Jubilee returned land every fifty years, dissolving accumulated debt by statute, a structural reset written into the constitution of Israel. The sabbath protected the worker and the animal and the foreigner by force of command. These are not charity. These are mishpat built into the architecture of the society, and they are the proof that biblical justice was always meant to touch systems and not merely soothe individuals. The charity view keeps tsedaqah and surrenders mishpat. It has half the verse.

Now steel-man the second amputation, the one that says justice is fundamentally political and structural. This view too is held by the faithful, and it too has deep warrant. It looks at the corners of the field and the Jubilee and says, correctly, that God legislated. God did not leave the poor to the unreliable kindness of the comfortable. He wrote law. He built the protection of the vulnerable into the structure so that it would not depend on whether anyone felt generous that morning. And the structural view sees what private charity is forever tempted to ignore, that a thousand acts of mercy can coexist with an iniquitous decree and never threaten it, that you can run the best soup kitchen in the city and the city will keep producing the hungry faster than you can feed them, because the production of hunger is structural. Abraham Heschel saw this with terrible clarity. The prophet's concern, he wrote, was not with petty wrongs but with the great catastrophe of the whole social order, and the prophet's God was not chiefly a being of metaphysical contemplation but a God of pathos who is personally outraged by injustice (Heschel 1962). The structural view protects the truth that God cares how the society is ordered, not merely how its individuals feel.

But the structural view also fails when it amputates. Make justice only political and you produce a righteousness that can hate. You can crusade for systemic change and despise every actual human being in your path, can want justice for the poor as an abstraction while feeling nothing for the poor man at your own gate, can build a movement that has mishpat as its banner and no hesed in its heart. Micah will not allow it. Do justice, and love kindness, and walk humbly. The same verse. The structural reformer who has lost humility has lost the third clause, and a justice that does not walk humbly with God becomes the libido dominandi wearing a halo, the lust to dominate dressed as liberation. Augustine warned that even the love of justice can be captured by the love of self, that we can crave the position of the one who sets the world right more than we crave the world being right (Augustine 426). The structural view keeps mishpat and risks losing both hesed and humility. It too has half the verse.

So here is the whole verse, and it judges both halves. Mishpat and tsedaqah, justice and righteousness, the rectifying flood and the right daily living that births it, held together, walked out humbly, warmed by hesed. Biblical justice is not charity and it is not politics. It is the restoration of shalom, the woven rightness of all things, and it requires both the bandage and the road, both the Samaritan and the repeal of whatever keeps filling the ditch (Plantinga 1995). The reason the church keeps tearing the two words apart is that each half is cheaper than the whole. The charity half costs my wallet but not my comfort with the system that fills my wallet. The political half costs my vote but not my heart, lets me love humanity while despising my neighbor. The whole costs everything. That is why we avoid it.

There is a history to how we lost this, and it is worth naming with some precision, because the amputation did not happen by accident. For long stretches of the modern Western church, especially after the revivalism of the nineteenth century, the word righteousness was steadily privatized. Tsedaqah, which in Hebrew meant living rightly in the whole web of your relationships and obligations, became in popular preaching a matter of personal piety, the state of an individual soul before God, measured by private morality and private devotion. The social, structural, covenantal weight of the word fell away. By the early twentieth century the split had hardened into a war. The fundamentalist modernist controversy of the 1910s and 1920s forced a choice that the Hebrew never permitted. One side took personal salvation and private righteousness and called the other side worldly. The other side took social reform and structural justice and called the first side escapist. The church divided its own vocabulary down the middle, handed mishpat to one party and tsedaqah to the other, and told each that the other half was a distraction. We are still living in the rubble of that divorce. When a congregation hears the word justice today and immediately files it under politics, or hears the word righteousness and immediately files it under private morality, that reflex is not biblical. It is the inheritance of a hundred year old quarrel that tore one Hebrew pairing into two warring slogans.

Now the reversal, and it lands on the pulpit first, on me. I have preached this verse and stopped at hesed, because hesed preaches warm and mishpat preaches expensive. I have told a congregation to love kindness and walked them right past the word that would have implicated our comfort, our zoning, our quiet arrangements that keep certain widows from certain gates. I did that. The prophets would have named me with the scribes, a writer who keeps writing the comfortable half. Heschel said the prophets were not interested in our religious feelings but in the cry from the gate, and I have too often offered the feelings and muffled the cry (Heschel 1962).

Which brings us, as everything finally does, to the cross, because the cross is where mishpat and tsedaqah meet and refuse to be cheapened. At Golgotha God does mishpat. He does not wave sin away. The bent thing is set right at full cost, the wrong is rectified, the verdict is rendered and the verdict is death. The law is satisfied before grace is spoken, because a justice that simply forgives without rectifying is not mishpat, it is indulgence, and God will not lie about what sin costs. And at the same cross God does tsedaqah. Paul's word for what happens there is the verb form of this very righteousness. God is just and the justifier of the one who has faith (Romans 3:26 ESV). He puts us in right relationship, the relational rightness tsedaqah always meant, by entering the ditch himself, becoming the beaten man on the road, paying the innkeeper with his own blood. The cross is mishpat and tsedaqah in a single body, justice and righteousness welded in the only place they were ever fully joined. Oliver O'Donovan argued that the resurrection vindicates the created moral order, that justice is not our invention to impose but God's order to recover, restored in Christ and entrusted to us as something to receive and not to seize (O'Donovan 1986). Which means I cannot do justice as a conqueror. I can only do it as a man who was himself the beaten one on the road, lifted by a justice I did not earn.

So when the church asks whether justice is charity or politics, the answer is that the question is a trap built to let us keep half. The widow at the gate does not need our theory. She needs mishpat, the verdict that matches reality and the provision that follows it. She needs tsedaqah, a people who live so rightly that her case was repaired before she ever had to plead it. She needs hesed, someone who knows her name. And she needs all three from people who walk humbly, who remember they were once beaten on the same road.

The gate is still there. The widow is still standing at the edge of it. And the word that comes out of that gate is still, somehow, up to us. Let justice roll down. The whole flood. Not half.

### Works Cited

Augustine. 426. The City of God. Translated by Marcus Dods. Edinburgh: T. and T. Clark.

Heschel, Abraham J. 1962. The Prophets. New York: Harper and Row.

Keller, Timothy. 2010. Generous Justice: How God's Grace Makes Us Just. New York: Dutton.

O'Donovan, Oliver. 1986. Resurrection and Moral Order: An Outline for Evangelical Ethics. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

Plantinga, Cornelius. 1995. Not the Way It's Supposed to Be: A Breviary of Sin. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

chapters.title: What the Bible Actually Says About Money
chapters.summary: The Bible refuses both the prosperity preacher who blesses your portfolio and the secular reader who reduces it to anti-wealth socialism, and the refusal is the point.
chapters.body:
A man once told me, after a funeral, that he had spent thirty years building something he could not take into the ground he was about to fill. He was not confessing greed. He was confessing surprise. He had played by every rule the culture handed him, and the rules had not lied to him about how to acquire, only about what acquiring would do to him. I have stood at enough gravesides to know that money keeps its promises and breaks them in the same motion. It delivers the house. It does not deliver the man who can live in it.

The question of what the Bible says about money is usually asked by someone who already suspects the answer and wants permission to dislike it. So let me name the real question first, because it is not whether wealth is allowed. The real question is whether money is a neutral tool that takes its moral color from the user, or whether money is a power, an active rival, something that wants you. The Bible answers that second question with a clarity that embarrasses most of our preaching. Money is not neutral. It has a name, and the name is mammon.

The spine of this whole matter runs through one passage, and I want to carry it the entire way. Paul writes to Timothy that godliness with contentment is great gain, that we brought nothing into the world and can take nothing out, and then the sentence everyone misquotes. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils. It is through this craving that some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many pangs (1 Timothy 6:6-10 ESV). Notice what Paul does not say. He does not say money is the root. He says the love of it is a root, one root among others, and that this love is not a vice on the surface of a life but a craving that reorganizes the whole interior around itself. The word he uses for craving describes a reaching, a stretch toward. Money is not the problem. The stretch is the problem. And the stretch is in me before it is in my bank.

Let me steel-man the two answers that want to silence Paul before he finishes.

The first is the prosperity teaching, and I will not caricature it, because at its best it gets something real. It says God is a Father who gives good gifts, that the creation is good, that poverty is not holy, that the dualism which treats matter as dirty and spirit as clean is a Greek lie the church absorbed and never coughed up. All of that is true. Israel's God made a world of vineyards and oil and wine and called it good before any human ruined it. The Scriptures are full of feasting. Abraham was rich. Job was restored. To pretend the Bible romanticizes destitution is to read it through a monk's bad day. The prosperity preacher is right that God blesses, and right that shame about the body and the field has done real damage. So I take the strongest form of it. God wants to bless His people, and He often blesses them with abundance.

The second answer comes from the other direction, the secular reduction that hears all this talk of the poor and concludes the Bible is simply an ancient socialism, a class document in religious dress, useful for guilt and nothing more. This reading also gets something right. It has actually read the prophets, which is more than many churchgoers can say. It has noticed that Amos thunders against those who sell the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals (Amos 2:6 ESV), that the Jubilee resets debt, that Jesus blesses the poor and warns the rich with a regularity that should unsettle anyone comfortable. The secular reader is right that the Bible is not indifferent to who has and who lacks. It is right that any Christianity which never disturbs the wealthy has not read its own book. So I take the strong form of that too. The Bible is dangerous to the comfortable, and it means to be.

Now watch what Paul's sentence does to both.

The prosperity teaching cannot survive verse nine, where the desire to be rich is itself the trap, where the wanting plunges people into ruin and destruction. Paul is not warning the rich here. He is warning the aspiring, the ones who want to be rich, which is nearly everyone reading this, including the man who writes it. The prosperity gospel takes the legitimate goodness of blessing and bolts a craving onto it, then baptizes the craving. It tells you the stretch is faith. Paul tells you the stretch is a hook. The two cannot both be true.

But the secular reduction cannot survive the passage either, because Paul does not abolish wealth, he disarms it. Three verses later he tells Timothy to command those who are rich, not to stop being rich, but to be rich in good works, generous and ready to share, storing up treasure as a foundation for the future (1 Timothy 6:17-18 ESV). That is not socialism, which seizes. That is not capitalism, which absolves. It is something the modern political menu has no item for. The rich remain rich and are commanded to bleed their wealth outward until it stops being theirs in any way that matters. The Bible does not nationalize the vineyard. It haunts the man who owns it.

So the answer to the real question is neither pole. Money is not morally neutral, which refutes the secular reduction, and money is not safely blessed, which refutes the prosperity preacher. Money is a power, and the only question is who serves whom.

Jesus said it without a single hedge. No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money (Matthew 6:24 ESV). Read it slowly. He does not say you should not. He says you cannot. It is not a prohibition. It is a description of a wiring that will not run two currents. And the word He chooses for money is not the ordinary coin. It is mammon, an Aramaic term He personifies as a rival lord. Jesus is not moralizing about budgets. He is naming a god with a small g and telling you it has applicants for your worship and a contract ready.

This is where the history matters, because the church has known this and forgotten it on a long cycle. In the fourth century, when Constantine's peace flooded the church with wealth it had never held, John Chrysostom preached in Antioch and Constantinople with a ferocity we have lost the stomach for. He told congregations of the newly comfortable that the rich man is a kind of thief, not because he stole, but because what he hoards is the bread of the hungry, the cloak of the naked, the coin owed to the poor (Chrysostom, Homilies on Lazarus). Not to share, Chrysostom said, is to rob. Preaching like that, year after year against the comfort of the powerful, was part of what set the imperial court against him and ended in his exile. We have softened it into a stewardship seminar.

The Reformers wrestled the same beast under the question of usury, the lending of money at interest, which the church had forbidden for over a thousand years on the authority of Scripture. By the sixteenth century commerce had outgrown the prohibition, and Calvin allowed interest within limits, not because he had grown lax but because he distinguished the productive loan from the predatory one. The distinction collapsed almost immediately, as such distinctions do, and within two centuries interest was simply the air the economy breathed. Jacques Ellul, the French theologian and sociologist, watched the end of that long erosion and named what we had done. Money, Ellul argued, is not a tool we picked up but a power we serve, and the modern person's pretense that it is neutral is precisely the lie that lets it rule (Ellul 1984). The man who insists his money is just a tool is the man the tool already owns.

Then came the move that finished us. In 1714, Bernard Mandeville published a poem and then a book, The Fable of the Bees, with the subtitle that should have been a warning, Private Vices, Public Benefits. His argument was simple and corrosive. Greed, vanity, the endless reaching, these private sins are the engine of public prosperity, and a society of saints would be a society of beggars. Adam Smith would later refine the insight into something gentler and truer, but the cultural residue was Mandeville's. We came to believe that the love of money, the very craving Paul called a root of evils, was the secret fuel of the common good. We did not reject Paul's diagnosis. We inverted it. We called the disease the cure.

And once a society decides its central vice is actually its engine, it needs a story about what money is for, a story that quiets the old warnings. Charles Taylor traced how the modern order came to imagine itself as a self-running economic mechanism, a great interlocking exchange in which each person pursuing his own gain produces, as if by design, the good of all (Taylor 2007). It is an elegant picture, and it is not entirely false. Markets do coordinate strangers across distances no charity could reach. But notice what the picture quietly accomplishes. It removes the moral question from the center of economic life and reassigns it to the edges, to private conscience, to what a man does with his surplus on a Sunday. The getting becomes neutral, even virtuous, and only the spending carries any weight. Paul will not allow that division. He locates the danger not in the spending but in the wanting, in the very motion the modern story has declared innocent. The love of money is a root, he says, and roots are underground, in the getting, where we have agreed to stop looking.

Wendell Berry has spent a working life refusing that agreement. He has argued that an economy which treats the love of gain as harmless will inevitably treat everything else, the land, the neighbor, the community, the body, as raw material for that gain, because once the central motion is exempted from judgment there is nothing left to limit it (Berry 1987). Berry writes as a farmer, which matters, because he has watched the abstraction do its work on actual ground, watched the family farm consolidated into the holdings of men who will never see it, watched the field Israel was told not to harvest to its edges reaped now to the very fencerow and beyond. He is describing in modern terms what Isaiah saw in the eighth century before Christ, the joining of house to house and field to field until there is no more room. The machinery is new. The hunger is the same hunger Paul named. It does not change across the millennia. Only its instruments grow more efficient.

And here is the reversal, the place where the objection, followed honestly, turns back toward the cross. The secular reader who says the Bible is just a class document has, without meaning to, paid the gospel a compliment. Because the reader is right that money is about power, right that the having and the lacking are never innocent, right that something is deeply wrong in the distance between the man with the vineyard and the man at his gate. The reader has seen the wound. What the reader has not seen is that the Bible saw it first, named it as sin and not merely as inequality, and refused the two cheap cures the world keeps offering. The world says, seize the vineyard, and calls it justice. The world says, bless the owner, and calls it grace. The gospel says something neither side can stomach. The vineyard owner is a debtor before God, and his only hope is the same as the beggar's.

Press the spine one more time before the cross, because Paul has not finished with us. He says the love of money pierced some through with many pangs, and the verb is worth sitting in. Pierced. Not disappointed, not distracted. Pierced, as a man is pierced who reached for something and was run through by it. This is the testimony of nearly every rich man I have buried and a good many I have counseled while they still had breath. The money did not fail to arrive. It arrived, and it kept arriving, and somewhere in the arriving the man discovered he had been hollowed out to make room for it, that the contentment Paul named at the start of the passage had been the one thing the wealth could not deliver and the one thing he had traded for it. We have all heard the sentiment that money cannot buy happiness, and we file it under platitude. Paul says something far worse. Money can buy the appetite for more money, and that appetite, fed, becomes the whole of a person. The hook does not let go. It sets deeper with every catch.

This is why the cross stands in the center of any honest theology of money, and not as a closing decoration. Gary Anderson has shown that in the biblical and later Jewish imagination, sin was understood as a debt, a weight recorded against the sinner, and that almsgiving to the poor was understood as the paying down of that debt, treasure stored in heaven in the most literal economic grammar (Anderson 2009). When Jesus tells the rich to store up treasure in heaven, He is not speaking in metaphor. He is telling them their accounts are in the wrong bank. And then He does the unthinkable. He pays the debt Himself. He who was rich, Paul says, for our sake became poor, so that we by His poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9 ESV). The richest sentence in the economy of God is a bankruptcy. The Son liquidates everything, down to the garment they gambled for at the foot of the wood, and the liquidation is the inheritance.

This is the law before the grace, and it must come in that order or it is sentiment. The law says the love of money has wormed into every one of us, the prosperity preacher and the prophet of equality alike, and that none of us serves the right master cleanly. The law says I have stretched toward security a thousand times in ways I dressed up as prudence. I have a family. I have five sons. The reaching wears the costume of love and is sometimes only fear. The law indicts the man who writes this before it indicts the man who reads it. Only after that indictment lands does grace mean anything, and then it means everything, because the debt I cannot pay has been paid in a currency I could not have minted.

So what does the Bible actually say about money. It says money is real, good, and dangerous, in that order and all at once. It says the goods of creation are gifts and not garbage, which silences the false holiness of poverty. It says the love of those goods is a root that grows in the dark, which silences the false holiness of wealth. It says you will worship something, and money is the most patient idol you will ever meet, because it never asks for worship in words. It only asks for your trust, a little more each year, until the day a man stands at a graveside and realizes he gave it everything and it gave him a house he is about to leave.

The contentment Paul names is not resignation. It is the freedom of a man who has already been bought, and so cannot be bought again. We brought nothing in. We will take nothing out. Between those two empty hands, the only question worth answering is whose we are. Mammon will take you on any terms. Christ has already paid for you in full. You cannot serve both. You were never able to.

### Works Cited

Anderson, Gary A. Sin: A History. New Haven: Yale University Press, 2009.

Berry, Wendell. Home Economics. New York: North Point Press, 1987.

Ellul, Jacques. Money and Power. Translated by LaVonne Neff. Downers Grove: InterVarsity Press, 1984.

John Chrysostom. On Wealth and Poverty. Translated by Catharine P. Roth. Crestwood: St. Vladimir's Seminary Press, 1984.

Taylor, Charles. A Secular Age. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 2007.

The Holy Bible, English Standard Version. Wheaton: Crossway, 2001.

chapters.title: What the Bible Says About Immigrants and Refugees
chapters.summary: Scripture commands love of the foreigner not as policy but as memory, and a people who forget the pit will always fear the stranger.
chapters.body:
I grew up without a father, which means I grew up knowing what it is to belong somewhere only conditionally. Not a stranger in a foreign country, nothing so severe. But close enough to the experience of standing at an edge, watching a household you are not quite inside, to make me suspicious of how easily settled people talk about who belongs. That suspicion is the only credential I bring to this subject. The Bible says a great deal about immigrants and refugees, and most of what it says is aimed precisely at people like the man I have become, comfortable, established, holding the keys to a house I did not build.

The real question is not whether Christians may hold views on immigration policy. They may, and faithful believers land in different places on enforcement and borders and law, and anyone who tells you Scripture dictates a particular statute is selling something. The real question is prior to policy and deeper than it. How does God regard the foreigner. What is the disposition of his heart toward the one who arrives with nothing, and what does he command of the people who claim his name. Settle that, and the policy arguments become arguments among people who have first agreed on what the stranger is worth.

The strongest objection is serious and I will not caricature it. It runs like this. The biblical commands about the ger, the resident alien, were given to ancient Israel about the legal sojourner, the one who entered the land lawfully and submitted to its covenant and its statutes. The ger was a documented resident, the argument goes, not a category that maps onto unlawful entry, and to flatten every distinction between the lawful immigrant and the unlawful is to misuse the text. Furthermore, the argument continues, Romans 13 establishes the legitimate authority of the governing power to maintain order and enforce law, and a nation has a real obligation to its own citizens, the duty of a household to its own. This is not a frivolous position. It guards two true things. Law matters, and a government does owe primary duties to those in its care. A serious reading of Scripture cannot wave those away.

But the strong objection runs into the wall of how much the law actually granted the ger, and the wall is high. Carry one text as the spine, the same one that exposed the engine of the whole code. 'You shall not wrong a sojourner or oppress him, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt' (Exodus 22:21 ESV). Notice the ground given. Not the sojourner's legal paperwork. Not his usefulness to the economy. The memory of Israel's own time as foreigners under Pharaoh. And notice how far the protection extends. The ger was to receive the same justice in court as the native born, the same sabbath rest, the gleanings of the field, a share in the festivals, even inclusion in the cities of refuge. 'You shall have the same rule for the sojourner and for the native, for I am the Lord your God' (Leviticus 24:22 ESV). The objection wants to limit the ger to the carefully documented. The law itself extends to him a near-equality the modern settled citizen would find radical if it were proposed today.

And the deeper answer reaches past statute into the marrow of who God says he is. 'He executes justice for the fatherless and the widow, and loves the sojourner, giving him food and clothing' (Deuteronomy 10:18 ESV). God does not merely permit the foreigner. He loves him, and feeds him, and the command to Israel is to imitate that love because they were objects of it first. Abraham Heschel saw that this was the prophetic nerve, that God's concern for the powerless was not one attribute among many but the revelation of his character. The greatness of a prophet, as Heschel described it, lay in the capacity to hold God and humanity together in a single thought, pleading for God before the people and for the people before God (Heschel 1962). The God of the prophets is not neutral toward the displaced. He is partisan toward them, and a people who claim him and fear them have not understood whom they worship.

Trace the history and Scripture turns out to be a record of refugees from beginning to end. Abraham was a wanderer who left Ur for a land not yet his. Jacob's family came to Egypt as economic migrants fleeing famine. The whole nation was born as a column of refugees walking out of slavery into a wilderness. Ruth was a Moabite immigrant, a foreigner of a despised people, who gleaned in Boaz's field under the very poverty laws written for the ger, and from that foreign woman came the line of David and the line of the Messiah. And the Messiah himself. Within two years of his birth, Matthew records, Joseph took the child and his mother and fled by night across a border into Egypt, escaping a king who meant to kill him. 'Rise, take the child and his mother, and flee to Egypt' (Matthew 2:13 ESV). The Son of God was a refugee child in a foreign land before he was anything else the world would later call him. The church that fears the refugee fears the infant it claims to follow.

Here is where the comfortable reader, and I am one, must feel the reversal. We instinctively cast ourselves as the settled householders deciding, from a position of ownership, whom to admit. We are the citizens. They are the strangers at the gate. Scripture takes that self-understanding and inverts it without apology. 'You are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God' (Ephesians 2:19 ESV). The word translated stranger and alien is the language of immigration. Before grace, we were the undocumented ones, with no standing in the commonwealth of God, no claim on the household, no right of entry. We did not earn citizenship in the kingdom. It was extended to us as pure amnesty, a status conferred on aliens who had no legal basis to demand it. Every Christian is a naturalized foreigner. We hold our place by grace and not by right.

The cross is where that amnesty was purchased, and it does the argument's hardest work. The law of the kingdom is exacting. None of us met its terms for entry. We arrived at its border with nothing, our papers a record of debt, no merit to present, no claim to make. The just verdict was exclusion, and it was deserved. Then Christ, the rightful Son, the one citizen with every claim, was himself cast outside the gate. 'So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood' (Hebrews 13:12 ESV). He was expelled, executed beyond the wall in the place of the unclean and the foreign, so that the excluded could be brought in. He took the position of the deported one so the deportable could become citizens. This is not a metaphor we may admire and set aside. It is the ground of our standing. We are inside the household only because the Son was put outside it.

Which leaves the settled Christian, leaves me, with a question that policy cannot answer and law cannot soften. The arguments about borders and enforcement are real, and I do not pretend the texts hand us a single statute. But underneath every such argument sits the prior thing, the disposition of the heart toward the one who arrives with nothing. And on that, Scripture is not ambiguous, and it is not gentle. We were sojourners. We were aliens with no claim, taken in by grace, given food and clothing and a place at a table we did not build. A people who remember the pit do not get to fear the stranger.

We loved him because he first loved us when we were the foreigners.

We are not permitted to forget the country we came from.

### Works Cited

Heschel, Abraham J. The Prophets. New York: Harper and Row, 1962.

The Holy Bible, English Standard Version. Wheaton: Crossway, 2001.

chapters.title: What the Bible Says About the Poor and the Stranger
chapters.summary: Scripture returns to the poor and the stranger hundreds of times, across law and prophets and Gospels, and the church has learned to read past every one of them.
chapters.body:
A man sleeps under the overpass two blocks from our church. I have driven past him on my way to preach about him. That is not a confession I enjoy making, but it is the truest sentence I can write to begin, because the question of what the Bible says about the poor is never first a question of exegesis. It is a question of who we have trained ourselves not to see. The text was never the problem. We were.

The real question is not whether Scripture cares about the poor. Even the most casual reader knows it does. The real question is why a book so relentless on this subject has produced a church so comfortable with poverty. Hundreds of passages across the law and the prophets and the Gospels touch wealth and want, the orphan and the widow, the laborer and the gleaner. We have read them and built sanctuaries with good parking. Something in us has learned to receive these texts as decoration rather than command.

The strongest objection deserves a fair hearing, because it is not stupid and it is not made only by the hard of heart. It runs like this. The biblical commands about the poor were given to a covenant nation, ancient Israel, a theocracy with specific agrarian laws for a specific people in a specific land. Gleaning laws assume fields. Jubilee assumes tribal allotment. The year of release assumes a shared bloodline. To lift these statutes out of Iron Age Canaan and drop them onto a modern pluralistic economy is, the argument goes, a category mistake. And the political reading of these texts has often been lazy, baptizing whatever policy the reader already preferred. That critique lands. The Bible is not a budget proposal, and people who quote Leviticus to win an election usually have not read Leviticus.

But here the strong objection breaks on a single word, and the word is ger. The sojourner. The stranger. The resident alien who belonged to no tribe, held no allotment, and stood outside the bloodline entirely. If the poverty laws were merely tribal housekeeping, the ger should have been excluded from them by definition. He is the one person the covenant could have ignored without contradiction. Instead he is named again and again, woven into the very statutes the objection says were for insiders only. 'When you reap the harvest of your land, you shall not reap your field right up to its edge, neither shall you gather the gleanings after your harvest. You shall leave them for the poor and for the sojourner' (Leviticus 23:22 ESV). The stranger gleans the same field as the widow. The law reaches past the boundary it supposedly defends.

This is the text I want to carry, because the ger exposes the engine underneath the whole code. Why include the outsider. The answer is given without argument, as a brute fact of Israel's identity. 'You shall love the sojourner, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt' (Deuteronomy 10:19 ESV). The memory of slavery is the foundation of mercy. Israel is commanded to treat the vulnerable as it wished it had been treated when it was vulnerable, when it had no land, no rights, no name worth recording in Pharaoh's ledgers. The poverty laws are not tribal property management. They are the moral residue of a rescue. A redeemed people remembers the pit.

The Hebrew has a word for the whole class of the unprotected, the anawim. The bowed-down ones. Abraham Heschel, reading the prophets, saw that their fury was never abstract. 'The prophet's word is a scream in the night,' he wrote, and while the world lies at ease and asleep, the prophet feels the blast from heaven (Heschel 1962). Amos does not condemn Israel for theological error in the seminary sense. He condemns men who 'trample the head of the poor into the dust of the earth' (Amos 2:7 ESV), who sell the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals. Isaiah indicts a worship that runs perfectly while the orphan goes uncared for, fasts that God refuses to smell because the fast he chose was 'to share your bread with the hungry and bring the homeless poor into your house' (Isaiah 58:7 ESV). The prophets did not separate the altar from the street. We did. That separation is our invention, not theirs.

Trace the historical root and the picture sharpens uncomfortably. The early church took these texts at face value in ways that scandalized Rome. By the fourth century the emperor Julian, who hated Christianity and tried to roll it back, complained in a letter around 362 that the 'impious Galileans support not only their own poor but ours as well.' The pagan world noticed Christians feeding strangers who were not theirs. Then came Constantine, then came land, then came endowment, and slowly the church that had been a refuge for the ger became a property owner with the ger outside its gates. The Reformers fought over grace and missed the poor. The American church, born in a land of seemingly endless property, baptized acquisition as blessing and read the poverty texts as metaphors for spiritual lack. We spiritualized hunger so we would not have to feed it. I have preached that sermon. I am inside this.

And here the reversal, because the gospel does not leave the comfortable reader where it found him. We imagine ourselves the gleaners, the generous ones with full fields choosing to leave a corner. Scripture will not let us keep that seat. The whole arc of redemption casts us not as the landowner but as the ger, the stranger with no claim, the bowed-down one who was 'alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world' (Ephesians 2:12 ESV). We are the sojourner. We did not earn our place at the table. It was given to us by a God who remembered our slavery when we had forgotten it ourselves.

This is where the cross does the argument's real work, and not as sentiment. The law demanded the gleaning, the open hand, the remembered pit, and we did not keep it. We reaped to the edges. We trampled heads into dust. The law's verdict on us is just, and it is severe, and we cannot answer it. So Christ became poor. 'For your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich' (2 Corinthians 8:9 ESV). He took the position of the anawim absolutely, naked on a Roman beam, executed outside the city wall where the unclean and the foreign were thrown. The one with every claim took the place of the one with none. Mercy to the poor is not a moral upgrade we add to faith. It is the faith, worked outward, because we have received exactly the mercy the poverty laws describe. We give what we were given. To withhold it is to forget Egypt.

The man under the overpass is still there tonight. I know his approximate location and not his name. The Bible says what it says about the poor and the stranger, with a clarity that does not require a scholar to decode, and the distance between that clarity and my life is not a gap in my theology. It is the gap. Heschel said the prophet's task was to make us feel the scream we had learned to sleep through. The text has done its work. The field still has corners.

We were sojourners in the land of Egypt. We are not allowed to forget it.

### Works Cited

Heschel, Abraham J. The Prophets. New York: Harper and Row, 1962.

The Holy Bible, English Standard Version. Wheaton: Crossway, 2001.
